what_it_does: When semiconductor manufacturers print circuits onto silicon wafers, the patterns on the physical mask (the 'stencil' used to expose the chip) do not transfer perfectly because of how light diffracts and scatters. Optical proximity correction (OPC) is the step where engineers pre-distort the mask patterns so that after the optical distortion, the printed result is what was intended. Modern chip designs increasingly require curved mask shapes rather than just rectangular polygons, but handling curves is mathematically difficult. This paper proposes representing curved mask edges using cardinal splines — smooth curves defined by a set of control points — which turns the OPC problem into adjusting those control points iteratively guided by a simulation of how light will print them. The method also enforces manufacturing rules (minimum widths, spacings, and curvature limits) and can start from the output of an inverse lithography solver (software that works backward from the desired print to a mask shape) and refine it to be manufacturable.
